tasks.objective: Establish precise symptom onset and blast radius. Determine exactly when payment-service error rate rose and when ledger write failures began (target ~14:55Z, 15 min after v6.0.0), whether the 60% error rate is isolated to the mandate flow / new ledger entry type or affects all payment paths, and whether other services that write to the ledger also show elevated errors/latency in the same window. Provide the error signature (status codes, exception messages, timeouts vs. validation rejects) and any resource trend on payment-service and ledger-service (CPU, connections, saturation).
tasks.answer: payment-service HTTP 5xx error rate rose sharply between 14:56Z and 15:00Z (0.19% → 60.15%), i.e. ~5 min after the stated ~14:55Z target, and stayed ~60–64% through 16:57Z. The failures are NOT isolated to the mandate flow or a new ledger entry type: every payment-service ERROR (59 in 14:30–15:20Z; 266 in 15:30–16:59Z) is the identical generic 'ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file: No space left on device'; a log search for 'mandate' returned zero matches. The root of the write failures is the database component 'ledger-db' (no 'ledger-service' exists), which hit 98% disk usage at 14:48:20Z and began throwing PANIC 'could not write to file pg_wal/xlogtemp...: No space left on device' at 15:01:01Z, with WAL ballooning from an inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' (33916 MB at 14:34Z → 77371 MB at 14:49Z) — a resource trend that begins ~35 min before the incident report. So blast radius is all payment paths that write to the ledger, and the DB is out of disk.

tasks.objective: Find what changed across ALL services in the 14:30–15:15Z window, not just payment-service: enumerate recent deployments (including payment-service v6.0.0), config/feature-flag changes, and any change to ledger-service, its schema, or shared infrastructure. Map the service dependency graph around payment-service to identify what payment-service depends on for ledger writes (which service/component actually persists the entry). Also search historical incidents for prior ledger write failures / new entry type rejections and their root causes.
tasks.answer: Across ALL services in the 14:30–15:15Z window the only change of any kind was the payment-service v6.0.0 release (dep-6203, deployed 14:46:00Z, adding a 'new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD' and mandate endpoints; rolled back 15:12:00Z); there were zero config/feature-flag changes anywhere, including on ledger-service. payment-service does not go through a ledger-service: for ledger writes it talks directly to ledger-db, a SHARED postgres (owner platform) that is also written to by order-service, portfolio-service and settlement-service — so a degradation in the shared ledger-db (or one of those neighbours) could equally explain the write failures. No historical incident shows a previously seen 'new entry type rejected' failure; past ledger-db write failures were disk/WAL, IOPS or failover related.

tasks.objective: Correlate the change list from task b against the exact onset time established by task a, and against the blast radius: determine whether any change other than payment-service v6.0.0 (e.g. ledger-service deploy, schema migration, shared config) lines up with onset, and assess whether rolling back v6.0.0 alone would clear the failures or whether a shared ledger-tier change is the actual trigger.
tasks.answer: No change other than payment-service v6.0.0 exists in the window, but v6.0.0 is not the trigger: the failure is disk/WAL exhaustion on the SHARED ledger-db, whose retained-WAL trend started ~14:34Z, ~12 min BEFORE the 14:46Z deploy, and which is written to directly by four services. Onset (14:56–15:00Z) tracks the ledger-db 98%-disk (14:48:20Z) and first PANIC (15:01:01Z), not the deploy. Rolling back v6.0.0 alone would not clear the failures — the freed disk would not return from a deploy rollback, as evidenced by errors continuing at 60% after the 15:12Z rollback.

What IS established: HIST-114's remediation is confirmed as "Dropped slot; added slot-lag alert" (resource_exhaustion), which concretely hardens the fix path, and the pre-dawn (00:00-05:00Z) and 13:00-14:40Z windows contain zero deployments and zero config changes — so the absence of a change in the 05:00-16:59Z deployment window does not by itself prove the slot went inactive spontaneously; it is simply unowned/unmonitored in the tooling. H1's first cause therefore rests on the ledger-db resource trend (F11/F16), not on a demonstrated consumer change.

critiques.summary: H1's mechanism is well grounded: F10/F11 (ledger-db 98% disk, WAL retention from inactive slot analytics_cdc growing 33916MB@14:34→77371MB@14:49, PANIC 'No space left on device' on pg_wal and base/ files at 15:01) are direct observations of the DB itself, and the payment-service error signature (F8/F9) is uniformly the propagated DB error — not mandate-specific. Temporal order favors H1: WAL growth precedes the 14:46Z deploy and onset (14:56–15:00Z) tracks the 14:48% disk/PANIC, and rollback did not clear errors (F17/F12) — H2 and H4 are properly contradicted by verbatim error text and the F9 zero-'mandate' log search. BUT the top hypothesis is over-confident at 0.82 because its central scope claim (a SHARED-DB origin affecting all four writers) rests entirely on inference from the shared:true flag and the error text, with zero co-writer evidence: no order-service/portfolio-service/settlement-service errors, no ledger-db metrics, and no proof that disk consumption is exclusively retained WAL. H3 currently ranks second and shares H1's observations; the one query that would actually separate them (co-writer blast radius) has not been run, so this is a specific, obtainable, decision-relevant gap. Also note H1's stated trigger=null sits oddly with F11, which the hypothesis itself leans on as the origin mechanism — an unverified actor swapped the slot into/out of activity at ~14:34Z, and that triggering change is nowhere in the change data (F2/F14). Not 'inconclusive': H1 and H3 name the same component (ledger-db), the same mechanism (WAL/disk exhaustion), and the same fix (free disk / drop slot), so the residual uncertainty is a confidence cap, not a fork in remediation.

challenges.issue: The scope claim 'the same ledger-db failure affects the other three writers' is explicitly an ASSUMPTION and is the only hop not backed by an observation. Without co-writer evidence, H1 cannot be distinguished from H3 (ledger-db infrastructure/volume/node fault) or from a failure that happens to be near ledger-db but not shared. The 0.82 confidence is not defensible for a hypothesis whose one untested link is precisely the link that separates it from the runner-up.

Disk consumption is attributed exclusively to retained WAL, but this is inferred from logs alone; no ledger-db disk-usage/WAL-size metric was ever queried (documented gap). If the volume is also being filled by something else, or if the WAL figure is a warning string rather than measured usage, the causal chain's first hop is unverified.

The mechanism's initiating event — replication slot 'analytics_cdc' becoming inactive/'inactive at ~14:34Z' — has no actor: no config change, no deployment, no documented consumer action explains why the slot stopped consuming WAL (F2/F14 = 0 changes). The trigger is declared null while F11 is simultaneously used as the origin, so the causal chain's true first cause is unexplained by all available change data.

H3 is listed as an active alternative at 0.35 but was not actively tested — it was retained only because ledger-db metrics were never queried. Its 'contradicting F5' is a HISTORICAL precedent (HIST-114, a different date), not evidence from this incident; using a past incident to contradict a live hypothesis is exactly the reasoning pattern the review standard forbids.

H2 rejection is sound (F8 error text is physical storage, F9 zero mandate logs, F17 rollback ineffective), but the schema-rejection arm was never positively excluded — the schema/ledger-service change enumeration came back EMPTY rather than 'searched and found nothing' (documented gap), so 'no schema change exists' may be inferred from an untracked change type rather than an actual absence.

critiques.summary: H1 is now well grounded and the alternatives that matter are contradicted by evidence. Each hop rests on VERIFIED observations of ledger-db itself: WAL retention from the inactive 'analytics_cdc' slot (33916MB@14:34:05Z → 77371MB@14:49:47Z, F11) → measured (not log-inferred) disk_used_pct 96.58%@14:20Z, ≥98%@14:38Z, 100.0%@14:56–14:59Z (F28) → Postgres PANICs on its own pg_wal and base/ files at 15:01:01/15:01:39Z (F10) → clients surface the verbatim 'No space left on device' (F8/F27). Temporal order is decisive and I verified it independently: WAL growth (14:34Z) and the 98% disk crossing (14:38Z) both precede the 14:46Z deploy and the 15:00Z onset, and the 100% crossing (≤14:59Z) precedes payment-service's first error (15:00:26Z), so the resource exhaustion cannot be caused by v6.0.0 (F16, F7, F29). Scope is now directly observed rather than inferred: order-service (47.78%) and settlement-service (54.04%) jump in the same 15:00Z bucket with the same disk signature, order-service's first error at 15:00:42Z — 16s after payment-service — confirming a shared-db origin (F24, F25, F27). H2 is properly dead: zero 'mandate' log matches anywhere (F9), the error text is a physical storage error not a schema/enum rejection, and rollback did not clear errors through 16:57:54Z (F17/F12). Remaining uncertainty is confined to ledger-db-internal detail, not to which component or which fix. Two residual issues cap confidence at 0.85 rather than higher: (a) portfolio-service (a co-writer) stayed flat at ~0.2% with zero 'space' matches (F26) — unexplained by a pure shared-db-fills-up story (e.g. different code path / retry / non-disk write path) — and its flatness was not verified to end-of-window; (b) H1's first cause (slot inactivity trigger) has no identified actor (F19–F23), which is a visibility gap, not a gap in the mechanism or the remediation. Neither changes the top hypothesis or the fix (free disk / drop slot per HIST-114), so this is accept with a confidence cap and assumptions, not a further round — especially with the time cost of another query cycle during a live SEV-1.

challenges.issue: portfolio-service is a direct ledger-db writer yet stayed at a ~0.2% baseline (max 0.30%) with ZERO 'space' ERROR-log matches over 14:20–16:59Z (F26), while the other two co-writers failed. A pure 'shared disk fills, all writers fail together' story predicts uniform failure; any writer-specific selectivity should be named (e.g. different write path, in-memory/queue buffering, retry, or a non-disk-bound query path). This is a scope gap in the causal chain, though it does not favor H2/H3/H4 (which predict no co-writer failure at all).

The first cause (slot 'analytics_cdc' becoming inactive at ~14:34Z) has no identified actor or owner (F19–F23). The chain therefore starts from an observed consequence with an unexplained trigger. This is a monitoring/ownership visibility gap, not evidence against the mechanism, but it means H1 explains the failure, not the onset trigger.

The WAL-size figures (33916→77371 MB) come from ledger-db log text; ledger-db exposes no WAL-size metric (available_metrics omit wal_size), so retained WAL being the dominant disk consumer is corroborated only by the disk_used_pct consequence, not independently measured.

Not fully excluded: no host/volume/IOPS telemetry exists to distinguish a hardware/volume fault from a retention-policy fill (H3 assumption). However it names the SAME component (ledger-db), SAME mechanism (disk/WAL exhaustion), and SAME fix path (free disk / drop slot), so its residual probability does not change remediation.

H5's distinctive claim (an unmanaged out-of-inventory consumer as the true origin) is unfalsifiable with current tooling and unobservable (F19–F23). It is retained at 0.20 largely on unfalsifiability rather than positive evidence; its remediation (ownership/monitoring) is additive to, not a substitute for, the slot-drop fix.

The schema-rejection arm of H2 is excluded only indirectly — by the physical-storage error text (F8/F10) and the zero 'mandate' log search (F9) — rather than by a positive record of a schema change. This is adequate for ranking (the storage evidence is decisive) but leaves a small inferential residue.
